parts.why: Counted on the sheet: A 3 woodpeckers, 6 pigs, 4 jaguars; B 3 nectarines, 3 blackberries, 6 apples. Keys right, legend pictures match the pile.
A 8 and 5, B 9 and 4; the key shows bundled tally marks; each form has a bundle of five.
A 9 seagulls (10 or 25), B 19 figs (10 or 20); one clearly better guess in each.
A 1 + 6 = 7, B 7 + 1 = 8; same kind.

Keys right (A 8 - 3 = 5, 6 - 3 = 3; B 8 - 1 = 7, 5 - 3 = 2), but Form B box 1 takes away only one dot (one less), easier than Form A box 1 (8 - 3). Fix: give B box 1 a take-away of 2 or 3, e.g. 9 - 3 = 6 or 7 - 2 = 5.

The lesson is 'Adding stories: some more come' (add to), but both stories are put-together stories (Ben has 3, Jack has 5, how many together; Zoe 6 and Lily 3), the same situation Part 5 tests, so add-to is never checked. Fix: A 'Ben has 3 strawberries. He picks 5 more. How many strawberries does Ben have now?' and B 'Zoe has 6 mangoes. Her mom gives her 3 more. How many mangoes does Zoe have now?'. The direction says Read, but in K the teacher reads it (see instruction).

Keys right (A 8 - 2 = 6, B 9 - 7 = 2), but 'There are 8 cherries on the table. 2 fall down.' is not natural US English: things fall off a table. Fix both forms: 'There are 8 cherries on the table. 2 roll off. How many cherries are still on the table?' (B: '7 roll off'). The direction says Read for a read-aloud K page (see instruction).
A 6 yellow + 4 red = 10 socks (none left white), B 2 blue + 6 green = 8 of 10 cups; color dots next to the color words help pre-readers.
One picture ON the box in each form (whale, apricot), the others beside and under.
3 dolphins and 3 kiwis to circle; keys right.
One clearly biggest owl (4th) and coconut (2nd), in different places.
Penguins 1-3-2 and bananas 2-3-1; the three sizes are clearly different.
AB patterns dog/koala and avocado/banana; next is dog and avocado; answers in different places.
Trace and write 7, 4 / 8, 3.
Counted: 9 elephants, 8 cats; 10 lemons, 7 apples. Keys right.
Color 3 of 8 turtles / 4 of 8 blackberries.
A 7 and 6 swans (spread row has fewer), B 8 and 7 apples; both 'no', one box per form.

Keys right (A 6 and 2, B 9 and 5), but Form B is clearly harder for a quick look: 9 in a 5+4 row against 6 in 3+3, and 5 against 2. Fix: give the forms the same sizes, e.g. A 6 and 4, B 7 (4+3) and 3, with choices one apart as now.
A 5 = 5 (star) and 5 sheep < 7 foxes (bottom); B 3 = 3 (star) and 6 apples > 3 avocados (top). Keys right.
3 vs 8 foxes, 8 vs 4 bananas; keys right.

Form B asks the same pair twice (8 and 4 in box 1, 4 and 8 in box 2), so box 2 is a copy of box 1; Form A uses 2 in both boxes. Also in both forms the two number cards run into the page footer: the bottom border sits on the line and 'Made with LessonCraftStudio.com' prints over it (enlarged page 3). Fix: B box 2 another pair (e.g. 3 and 7), A box 2 without 2 (e.g. 5 and 9), and make the cards shorter or move Part 8 up so it clears the footer.
Circle, skinny triangle / turned rectangle, turned square; one right name each.
Enlarged: hexagon 6, octagon 8, trapezoid 4 / pentagon 5, heptagon 7, triangle 3.

Keys right (pyramid to the solid bin, rectangle to the flat bin), but each form has ONE shape and two bins, so a guess scores half the time, and the direction says 'each shape'. Fix: put three or four shapes in each form, flat and solid mixed (e.g. A pyramid, circle, cylinder; B rectangle, cube, cone), and keep the bins labeled with the square and the cube.
Cone to party hat, cylinder to can; one match each.

Enlarged: both keys are right (two triangles and a turned square), but Form B is Form A turned upside down, the same shape with the same cuts, so B asks exactly what A asks. Fix: give Form B a different shape made of two triangles and a square (e.g. a big triangle or a rectangle).
Counted: 17 koalas, 14 tigers; 18 coconuts, 13 limes, in rows of five.
Keys right (6 + 2 = 8, 8 + 1 = 9), but Form B counts on only one (just 'the next number'), easier than Form A's two. Fix: B 7 on the box and 2 bananas (9), or 8 and 2 (10).
5th leopard and 6th blackberry from the arrow; keys right.

Keys right (7 + 3, 5 + 5), but Form B is the easiest partner of 10 (a full top row, doubles 5 + 5), easier than Form A's 7 + 3, and its answer 5 is also the answer of Part 2 just before it. Fix: B 8 + ? = 10 (answer 2); avoid 6 + 4, which is Part 4 of Form B.
Worked every shape: A 10-3, 1+6 green; 1+2, 9-6 blue; 2+6, 3+5 yellow. B 7-3, 9-5 blue; 3+4, 8-1 yellow; 3+7, 4+6 green. Text in the shapes readable when enlarged.
9 odd, 8 even; keys right. The leftover jaguar sits alone in a dashed box on the child's page, so it is close to given away, but that is the K pairing scaffold the direction describes.
8 - 2 = 6, 9 - 2 = 7 with the given-away pictures crossed out.
16 - 6 = 10 and 17 - 14 = 3 (part unknown); keys right. The key writes the answer in the bar where the child is told to write '?' (see notes).

Keys right (17 - 5 = 12, 16 - 10 = 6), but 'Some pears get lost. ... How many pears got lost?' switches tense and pears do not 'get lost' naturally. Fix: A 'Emma had 17 pears. She gave some to her friends. Now she has 12 pears. How many pears did she give away?', B the same with 16 and 6 pomegranates.
13 vs 6 = 7, 11 vs 6 = 5, rows lined up; keys right.
7 + 4 + 6 = 17 and 4 + 8 + 6 = 18; the key marks the pair that makes ten.
The key does not draw the hands: each clock is empty with only '10:00' written small on the face. Fix: draw the short hand on 10 and the long hand on 12 (A 10:00, 3:00; B 5:00, 8:00) in the key.
Enlarged: A clocks 6:30, 5:30, 6:00, B 5:30, 5:00, 4:30, hour hands correctly between the numbers; no clock sits above its own time.

Form B uses Monday and Tuesday, so box 1's answer 'Tuesday' is printed as today in box 2 and box 2's answer 'Monday' is printed in box 1: each box shows the other's answer. Form A (Thursday, Sunday) has no such overlap. Fix: B today Monday and Friday (Sunday/Tuesday, Thursday/Saturday).
Four missing ordinals in each form; keys right. A has to write 2nd and 3rd, B only 3rd, a small difference.

Sums are right (20, 12 / 21, 11), but the direction says 'in each purse' and no purse is drawn, and the coins are plain circles with 10, 5 and 1 printed on them, so the child only adds the printed numbers. Fix the direction (see instruction); better still, draw real dime, nickel and penny faces at relative size and leave the values off, since naming the coins is what Grade 1 coin lessons teach.
Enlarged: 1 ten + 6 ones = 16, 1 ten + 7 ones = 17.
6 tens = 60, 7 tens = 70.
64 and 63; keys right (the two forms are very close, see notes).

Keys right, but Form A box 2 (9 with nine, ten, eleven) is easy because nothing else looks like 'nine', while Form B box 2 (8 with seven, eighteen, eight) has the real trap eighteen. Fix: A box 2 'nine, nineteen, five'.

Keys right (88, 79, 29 = 3, 2, 1; 43, 66, 14 = 2, 3, 1; 57, 36, 89 = 2, 1, 3; 41, 68, 67 = 1, 3, 2), but in Form A every number has a different tens digit, while Form B box 2 has 68 and 67, where the ones decide. Fix: give Form A one box with the same tens, e.g. 43, 66, 63 (1, 3, 2).
Enlarged: one real triangle (the curved and four-sided shapes are not); one real square (the slanted one, the rectangle and the square with a gap are not).

On the child's page the squares under the fish (6) and the papaya (7) are already shaded teal and the rest are white, so the child just counts the colored squares and never decides where the object ends. Fix: print all ten squares white on the check page; keep the shading only in the key.
Enlarged: A box 1 has two gaps, B box 1 starts after the ribbon end and runs past the other end (both wrong), box 2 right in both; keys ring the mistakes.

This does not test sorting: each card is one picture (penguin, camel, blueberry, raspberry) and one of the three bins is labeled with the very same picture, so it is picture-to-identical-picture matching that every child gets right. Fix: give each form one card with 6 to 9 mixed pictures to sort into the three bins and count each bin, or label the bins with a category (birds / fish / mammals; berries / citrus / other) using pictures that differ from the items.
Cats 6, antelopes 4; oranges 6, pomegranates 5.
Raccoon 5, koala 6; pineapple 6, blackberry 2.

Child's page is right (woodpecker, penguin, moose pattern: woodpecker and moose missing; fig, kiwi, nectarine: nectarine and kiwi missing). The Form B key labels the two empty boxes '7' and '8' (Form A uses 1 and 2), which a teacher will read as numbers to write. Fix: label them 1 and 2 in the Form B key.
A: only the circle in halves is equal; B: circle in halves and rectangle in halves equal, the thin-wedge circle is not.
32 + 47 = 79, 60 + 16 = 76; no regrouping in either.

Keys right, but Form A needs regrouping (46 + 37 = 83) and Form B does not (27 + 60 = 87, a multiple of ten), and 60 also starts Part 1 of Form B. Fix: B 'Leo takes 28 down. Now there are 59 figs left' (87, regrouping).
69 + 11 = 80 (more) and 77 - 42 = 35 (fewer); the dashed piece sits on the shorter bar in both keys.

Keys right (89, 78 / 86, 47), but (1) the story starts with a stray '1.' in Form A and '3.' in Form B, left over from the worksheet; (2) Form B regroups in step 2 (86 - 39) while Form A regroups nowhere (89 - 11); (3) the equations a) 68 + 21 = and b) _ - 11 = are printed, so a child can ignore the story. Fix: remove the numbers, A 'Mia puts in 23 more. Then Mia takes out 14.' (91, 77), and print only empty boxes with the sign for the child to choose.

Keys right (A 6 and 7, B 3 and 2), but Form A has bundled tallies (5 + 1, 5 + 2) and Form B only 3 and 2 single strokes, much easier. The 'plum' row shows a red apple (key label says plum). Fix: B counts with a bundle of five (e.g. 6 and 8) and use a plum picture or label it apple.
Keys right, but Form B uses the same two counts as Form A (7 and 4, just swapped). Fix: B counts 5 and 8.
Brown E3-E6 / pink F3, F4, E2, F1; one color group each.
Counted X marks: 5, 4, 2 / 4, 5, 3.
Most common length 6 (three times) and 5 (four times); keys right.
1 dolphin = 2, 6 reindeer = 12; 1 coconut = 2, 7 nectarines = 14 (scale of 2 is a Grade 3 standard, see notes).
Enlarged: ticks by ones, arrows at 47 and 59 / 41 and 53.
75 to 83, 55 to 47 / 84 to 74, 54 to 46, walked step by step.
17 + 47 = 64 and 13 + 48 = 61, both regroup.

Keys right (58 - 24 = 34, 57 - 12 = 45), but both forms have enough ones ('yes'), so the lesson's skill, opening a ten, is never needed, and no box anywhere in the check subtracts with regrouping. Fix: A 52 - 27 = 25, B 61 - 34 = 27 (both 'no', the child opens a ten).
16 + 33 = 49, 49 - 45 = 4 / 26 + 51 = 77, 79 - 15 = 64; no regrouping in either form.

All six sums right (96, 52, 85 / 79, 87, 62), but the direction tells the child to write the new ten in the small box above the tens and the key leaves that box empty. Fix: show 1 in the carry box in all six key boxes.

Counted: 65 + 11 = 76 and 34 + 44 = 78, right, but in a within-1,000 unit both are two-digit with no new ten, Grade 1 work. Fix: use block groups that make a new ten (e.g. A 46 + 27 = 73, B 38 + 45 = 83) or add hundreds flats.
Keys right (180 + 563 = 743, 136 + 785 = 921), but Form A regroups once and Form B twice. Fix: A 186 + 567 = 753 (two regroupings) or B with one. The key leaves the carry boxes empty; show the 1s.
Counted: 67 - 31 = 36 and 48 - 11 = 37, right, but two-digit with no ten to break. Fix: A 52 - 27 = 25, B 63 - 36 = 27 drawn with blocks.
675 - 180 = 495 and 728 - 156 = 572, each regroups the tens once.

Keys right (57 + 43 = 100, 75 + 35 = 110), but these are two-digit sums, Grade 2 work, in a within-1,000 Grade 3 unit, and nothing is subtracted. Fix: A 457 + 368 = 825, B 584 + 279 = 863, and add a subtraction box with regrouping in each form (e.g. 702 - 358 = 344, 615 - 287 = 328).

Form B is 16 + 4 = 4 + ?, so the child copies 16 from the other side; Form A 15 + 4 = 14 + ? is different and both are Grade 1 numbers. Fix: B 16 + 4 = 15 + ? (5), or at Grade 3 level A 245 + 30 = 240 + ? (35), B 318 + 40 = 310 + ? (48).

Keys right (669 + 664 odd, 674 + 380 even), but 'tick' is British (US: check or fill in), and the table lists 'even + odd = odd' but not 'odd + even', which is exactly Form A's case (9 + 4) while Form B (4 + 0) is in the table. Fix: add 'odd + even = odd' to the table and use the instruction below.

Keys right (203, 590 / 187, 448), but the stories start with stray numbers ('1.' in A, '2.' in B, left over from the worksheet), and the equations a) 551 - 348 = and b) _ + 387 = are printed, so a child gets full marks without reading the story, which is the skill of the unit. Fix: remove the numbers and print only empty boxes for the two steps.

Keys right (27, 59 / 21, 52), but both forms multiply and nothing in the whole check divides, in a unit called all four operations; stray '2.' / '1.' and printed equations as in Part 1. Fix: make each form a divide step, e.g. A 'Jack has 36 cherries. He puts them equally into 4 bags and gives 1 bag to Ben. How many cherries does Jack have left?' (9, 27), B the same with 42 lemons and 6 bags (7, 35).

Answers right (218 + 188 + 297 = 703, estimate 700; 341 + 193 + 279 = 813, estimate 800), but the key shows only n = 703 / 813. Fix: show the equation (218 + 188 + 297 = n) and the estimate (200 + 200 + 300 = 700) in the key.
One right angle among obtuse and acute angles in each form.

Keys right (parallelogram, trapezoid: not a rectangle), but each form has one shape, both answers are 'not a rectangle', and the direction's 'Squares are rectangles too' has no square to apply to. Fix: three or four shapes per form, e.g. A square, parallelogram, turned rectangle; B rectangle, trapezoid, turned square.
Turned square 4, hexagon 6, rectangle 2 / pentagon 5, square 4, triangle 3; the shapes are regular.
6 pandas = 30, 2 fish = 10; 7 pineapples = 35, 3 blackberries = 15.

Counts right (2, 5, 3 / 1, 5, 4), but every X sits on a whole number and the questions ask only about whole numbers, so the half marks of 'A line plot with halves' are never read. Fix: put Xs above 1 1/2 and 2 1/2 and ask about them in both forms.

Enlarged: the pencils end at 1 1/2 and 3 3/4, keys right, but Form A lands on a half-inch mark and Form B on a quarter-inch mark, which is the skill of the lesson. Fix: A pencil ending at 1 3/4 or 2 1/4.
Eighths in both forms; A one equal circle, B equal circle and equal bar; the uneven bar and circle are clear.
1/6, 3/4 / 5/6, 2/3; none can be written with smaller numbers.
1/4 to the bar of 4, 1/5 to the bar of 5.
Enlarged: 6, 4, 8 and 3 equal parts; dots at 1/6, 1/4, 1/8, 1/3 (unit fractions, as the lesson says).
3/6 and 4/6; the off-by-one wrong answer (4/6, 5/6) is among the choices.
1/3 vs 1/6 and 3/6 vs 3/4, same top number, bars the same length; the answer is left in A and right in B.

Keys right (4/6 = 2/3, 1/3 = 2/6, 2/8 = 1/4; 4/6 = 2/3, 1/2 = 2/4, 1/4 = 2/8), but Form B picture 1 is the same bar as Form A picture 1 (6 parts, 4 shaded, matched to 2/3). Fix: B picture 1 another fraction, e.g. 6 of 8 shaded matched to 3/4.
1/3 of 6 moose = 2, 1/3 of 9 limes = 3.

checks.why: All keys right and the forms match. Note for the teacher page: the days of the week (in the title) and 'Which is heavier?' are not in the check.
Keys right, but Part 3 tests put-together twice instead of add-to, Part 4 needs natural wording, and Form B box 1 of Part 2 is easier.
Every part has one right answer, clear pictures and the same level in both forms.
Keys right; Part 8 repeats a pair in Form B and runs into the footer, and Part 5 is harder in Form B.
Keys right; the flat-or-solid part is a single coin-flip shape, and the tangram shape in Form B is Form A upside down.
Keys right; only the count-on box in Form B (+1) needs to match Form A.
Keys right; Part 3 Form B (5 + 5) is easier than Form A and repeats the answer of Part 2.
All keys right and the forms match; the 'get lost / got lost' story wording needs fixing.
The key draws no clock hands, Form B days print each other's answers, and the coin part names a purse that is not there and prints the coin values.
Keys right; Parts 4 and 5 are easier in Form A than in Form B.

Ruling lifted: graphs and sorting are now in the check (8 of 9 lessons), but the sorting part is identical-picture matching and the measuring part shades the answer squares; with those two fixed the check is fair to the unit.
Keys right; Form B regroups less often than Form A and the two-step story has stray numbers and printed equations.
Keys right; Form B tally counts are much smaller with no bundle, and Form B Part 2 reuses Form A's counts.
Keys right, but no box needs subtraction with regrouping (Part 4 is 'yes, enough ones' in both forms) and the carry box is empty in the key.

Ruling lifted: three-digit adding and subtracting with regrouping is now tested in both forms, so the check is fair; the block parts are still two-digit without a new ten and the adding part is unequal between forms.
No rounding at all (three of the seven lessons, the first word of the title), no subtraction, and the only computation is two-digit Grade 2 work; Form B of 'Make it balance' can be copied.
Keys right, but nothing divides, the steps are printed so the stories need not be read, and stray story numbers remain.
Keys right; the rectangle part is one shape per form, the half-unit line plot never uses halves, and the ruler part is easier in Form A.
All earlier problems are fixed and every key is right; only Form B of Part 7 repeats Form A's first picture.

instruction.G1-238: Listen to the story. Use the pictures to help you. Write the answer in the box.
instruction.G1-239: Listen to the story. Use the pictures to help you. Write the answer in the box.
instruction.G2-244: Draw a line from each shape to the right bin. Flat shapes go to the square bin. Solid shapes go to the cube bin.
instruction.G1-228: Add up the coins in each box. Write how many cents in all.
instruction.G1-139: Each object sits on a row of unit squares. Count the squares from one end of the object to the other. Write the length.
instruction.G1-381: Read the name. Circle every shape that really is that shape.
instruction.G3-386: Do not add. Look at the underlined ones digits and use the table. Fill in the circle to show if the sum is odd or even.
instruction.G3-359: Add one place at a time. Start with the ones. Regroup when you need to.
instruction.G3-361: Add one place at a time. Start with the ones. Regroup when you need to.
instruction.G2-502: Subtract one place at a time. Start with the ones. Regroup when you need to.
instruction.G3-340: Is each shape a rectangle? Remember, a square is a rectangle too. Draw a line from each shape to the right box.
instruction.G3-493: Each pencil lies on its own ruler. Write its length to the nearest quarter inch. The rulers are drawn smaller than a real ruler.
instruction.G2-511: Read the story. Do the first step, then the second step. Write the numbers in the boxes.

notes: Read all 19 dumps and every contact sheet. Enlarged (and deleted afterwards): k-counting-to-10 page 3 bottom (Part 8 overlapping the footer); k-shapes Parts 2, 3, 5 (sides, bins, tangram cuts); k-putting-together-number-bonds page 3 (code shapes and pairs); g1-time-calendar-coins clocks (Part 1 key, Part 2 hands) and coins; g1-shapes-measuring-graphs Parts 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 on check and key pages; g2-graphs-and-grids Part 1 (the 'plum' is an apple); g2-adding-and-subtracting-within-100 Part 1 ticks and Part 6 carry box; g2-add-subtract-within-1000 block counts; g3-rounding Part 3 child page (both circles, no tell); g3-shapes-and-data rulers (pencil tips at 1.51 and 3.75 inches); every page of g3-fractions (ticks, parts and shading counted).

Bar-model keys (g1-story Parts 2-3, g2-story Parts 1-3) write the answer number in the bar where the direction tells the child to write a question mark; teachers should accept '?' there, and either equation (6 + 10 = 16 or 16 - 6 = 10) should be accepted. A note on the key would help.
Many one-card parts say 'each story', 'each shape', 'each pencil' or 'in each row'. Harmless when read aloud, but 'the story' is cleaner where there is one card.

Grade fit at the unit level (the check only mirrors the unit): odd and even in K (Part 6 of number bonds) is CCSS 2.OA.C.3; the pre-paired pictures make it doable. A scale of 2 in a picture graph (g2-graphs Part 6) is 3.MD.B.3. Lines of symmetry (g3-shapes-and-data Part 3) are 4.G.A.3. Coins in Grade 1 are not CCSS (2.MD.C.8) but are common in US first grade.

g2-adding-and-subtracting-within-100 Part 1 key: the answer numbers are printed twice slightly offset (two copies of 47, 59, 41, 53 in the key PDF text), so they look smudged; the child page is clean.
g1-tens-and-ones Part 3: Form B (63) is Form A (64) minus one cube, and Form A shows 6 tens in Parts 2 and 3; acceptable, but a different tens digit in one form would make A and B more independent.
g1-story-problems-within-20 and k-adding: the crossed-out pictures in the take-away stories show the answer directly; fine for the within-10 lesson.
